rationale: A wins because it knows where the cliff edge is. It keeps the clean, grounded launch story in "Linear, the engineers' issue tracker, now wants the whole product org," then tells the founder which proof gaps kill the softer angles. B walks straight into the trap A correctly refused: "taking on the product-management stack" and "territory owned by incumbent product-management suites" invent a category fight the update did not supply.
gaps_in_A: "Linear is betting it can grow into product teams without a sales team" overstates an omission; the update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned, not that none exists.
"category-creation" is a little grand for a product expansion; the actual angle is boundary crossing, not a new category.
"A keyboard-first tool built for engineers is now pitching itself to designers" is labeled customer-story, but no named customer or beta user exists yet. A flags the gap, but this is not pitch-ready.
gaps_in_B: "taking on the product-management stack" invents a competitive fight; the update gives no competitors, incumbent names, switchers, or market-share claim.
"territory owned by incumbent product-management suites" is dressed-up hallucination. Its own proof request admits the premise is missing.
"three viable shapes exist" is too generous; the counterposition angle should be held until Linear names the tools it expects PMs to leave.
"trend" is loose on the design angle. One launch can support a craft question, not a trend claim without more examples.
